omu0: Calcific Tendinopathy of the Shoulder: Symptoms, Treatment and Exercises | İhsan Eren
omu1: Sudden severe shoulder pain and calcium seen on an X-ray? What is calcific tendinopathy, does it go away on its own, and which treatments are available? Warning signs and six exercises to do at home.
omu3: Do you have severe shoulder pain that came on suddenly and keeps you awake at night, or did an X-ray show “calcium”? A build-up of calcium in the tendons around the shoulder is called calcific tendinopathy. The pain can be very intense, but it is not a serious or harmful condition; most calcium deposits disappear on their own over time.

omu18: You can take painkillers or anti-inflammatory medicines after checking with your doctor or pharmacist. Ice packs can also ease the pain.
omu19: Take things a little easier for the first few weeks and change activities that make the pain worse.
omu21: Move your shoulder as far as the pain allows; this prevents stiffness. Use a sling only briefly, for comfort.
omu23: Once the severe pain has settled, move on to stretching and strengthening exercises. If symptoms persist, physiotherapy can help.
omu24: Six exercises to free up the shoulder step by step
omu25: Start with the first three exercises. As the pain begins to ease, usually after 2–3 weeks, add the others. Move within your natural range without forcing; the exercises should not increase your symptoms.
omu26: Lean forwards, resting your good hand on a table. Let your painful arm hang loosely and gently sway your body so the arm makes small circles. Don’t use your muscles to force the arm.
omu27: 1–2 minutes in total, 4–5 times a day
omu29: Sit or stand tall. Without lifting your shoulders, draw them back and slightly down so your chest opens.
omu32: Let your arm rest comfortably by your side. Bend your elbow fully within a pain-free range, then straighten it fully. A gentle stretch is enough; don’t push into pain.
omu34: Sliding the arm up the wall
omu35: Stand facing a wall and rest the forearm of your painful arm against it. Slide your arm up the wall within a pain-free range, then slowly lower it.
omu36: 10 repetitions, 4–5 times a day (after the first 2–3 weeks)
omu37: Keep the elbow of your painful arm tucked into your side and bent to 90 degrees. Hold a stick in both hands; push with your good arm to slowly move the forearm of your painful arm outwards.
omu38: Hold for 5 seconds, 10 repetitions (after the first 2–3 weeks)
omu39: Pushing outwards against a door frame
omu40: Keep your elbow bent to 90 degrees and close to your body. Rest the back of your hand against a door frame and gently push outwards without moving your arm.
omu41: 5 seconds, 10 repetitions (once the pain has eased)
omu42: An X-ray showed calcium; is that the cause of my pain?
omu43: Not always. Calcium deposits in the shoulder tendons are also found in about 8% of adults without any symptoms. So calcium on an X-ray does not by itself show what is causing the pain; it needs to be assessed together with an examination.
omu44: Does the calcium go away on its own?
omu45: Most calcium deposits disappear on their own over time. The severe pain often settles within a few weeks, but it can take 9 months or longer for the calcium to dissolve completely, and milder pain may continue during this time.
omu46: Why did the pain suddenly become so severe?
omu47: Sudden, very severe pain often comes when the body starts to reabsorb the calcium. So however hard this phase is, it is often part of healing.
omu49: The first step is controlling the pain and keeping the arm moving as far as the pain allows. If the pain does not settle, your doctor may suggest a steroid injection, breaking up and washing out the calcium with a needle under ultrasound guidance (lavage), or shockwave therapy. A review found that lavage may be more effective than shockwave therapy or a steroid injection alone, but the quality of the evidence is low. Surgery is kept for the rare cases where pain cannot be controlled in other ways.
omu51: Use a sling only briefly, for comfort, and stop as soon as you can. Moving your shoulder without increasing the pain prevents stiffness. Sleeping propped up on pillows may be more comfortable.
omu52: For pain that increases when you lift your arm out to the side, see the shoulder impingement guide; for gradually increasing stiffness, see the frozen shoulder guide.
